figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Behavior–Capability frontier protocol. (A) Contrastive examples define layer-wise CAA directions, after which the intervention layer is selected using behavioral validation. (B) At the fixed layer, coefficients are evaluated for directional behavioral gain subject to simultaneous capability constraints. The feasible coefficient with the largest directional behavioral gain defines the operating point. (C) The operating point is frozen before independent behavioral and capability confirmation and all post-selection audits.
figures.headline: The protocol fixes the layer on behavioral validation, then freezes the feasible coefficient before any held-out or capability confirmation.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Behavior-selected intervention depth. Each panel reports $\ell_{b}^{*}$ for the seven behaviors as fractional model depth. Llama 2, Llama 3.1, and Mistral select intermediate layers; Qwen2.5 selects consistently later layers.
figures.headline: Selected intervention layers cluster at intermediate depth for three models and at later depth for Qwen2.5.
citing_sentences: Qwen2.5 shifts later, selecting layers 17–19 of 28, roughly $0.63$–$0.70$ of model depth (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Held-out survival of frozen frontiers. $R_{B}$ denotes behavioral support, $R_{C}$ capability-holdout survival, and $R_{J}$ their conjunction among nonzero operating points. The strict $1\%$ budget is difficult to preserve on capability holdout; survival rises sharply at $3\%$ and changes little at $5\%$.
figures.headline: Capability holdout is hard to pass at the 1% budget, where survival rises sharply at 3% and changes little at 5%.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Steering-vector geometry and causal transfer. Signed cosine similarity is positively associated with signed cross-behavior transfer under equal-$\eta$ interventions, but the relationship is highly dispersed.
figures.headline: Signed cosine similarity is positively associated with signed cross-behavior transfer, but the relationship is widely dispersed.
citing_sentences: Across all 1176 ordered transfer measurements, signed cosine similarity is positively associated with signed causal transfer ($\rho_{\mathrm{S}}=0.290$, exact permutation $p=1.98\times 10^{-4}$; Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Open-ended behavioral response under frozen steering. Mean blinded judge score on a 0–4 target-behavior scale for negative steering, baseline, and positive steering. Error bars show 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. Sycophancy remains ordered; refusal and hallucination do not show the same bidirectional pattern.
figures.headline: Open-ended sycophancy scores rise monotonically from negative to positive steering, while refusal and hallucination lack the same bidirectional pattern.
citing_sentences: For sycophancy, mean target-behavior score increases monotonically from $1.35$ under negative steering to $2.29$ at baseline and $2.77$ under positive steering (Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Full-layer behavior localization across models. Each panel shows the coarse behavioral separation $B_{b}(+1,\ell)-B_{b}(-1,\ell)$ for all seven behaviors across decoder layers. Outlined squares mark the final behavior-selected layers $\ell_{b}^{*}$ obtained after the subsequent dense local layer–coefficient search. Steering response is concentrated within model-specific depth bands, with Qwen2.5 exhibiting a systematically later intervention region.
figures.headline: Coarse all-layer scans show large bidirectional separation concentrated in model-specific depth bands, with Qwen2.5 in later layers.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows the coarse separation $B_{b}(+1,\ell)-B_{b}(-1,\ell)$ across all behaviors and layers.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Selected-layer behavior–capability coefficient responses. For each model, the upper heatmap reports the behavioral change $\Delta B_{b}(\alpha,\ell_{b}^{*})$ across the coefficient grid at the behavior-selected layer. The lower heatmap reports the conservative capability margin $\min_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\operatorname{LCB}_{95}[\Delta A_{k}(\alpha,\ell_{b}^{*})]$ over MMLU, ARC-C, and HellaSwag. A coefficient is feasible at budget $\varepsilon$ when this margin is at least $-\varepsilon$. These response surfaces are the inputs to capability-constrained coefficient selection.
figures.headline: At the selected layer, sign-specific coefficient grids pair behavioral gains with conservative capability margins that gate feasibility.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 compresses these 28 model–behavior response surfaces.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Frozen operating points across capability budgets. Each panel reports the selected raw coefficient $\alpha^{*}$ and signed residual-relative strength $\eta_{\mathrm{s}}^{*}$ for every behavior, steering direction, and budget. Zero cells correspond to a frontier that retains the unsteered model.
figures.headline: At the 1% budget, 32 of 56 frozen claims select zero coefficient; at 3% only one does, and none at 5%.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows the selected coefficient $\alpha^{*}$ and signed residual-relative strength $\eta_{\mathrm{s}}^{*}$ for every behavior, direction, budget, and model.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Limiting protected capability benchmark. Counts identify which benchmark attains the minimum capability lower bound at frozen frontier operating points. The limiting benchmark varies across models and budgets.
figures.headline: The limiting protected benchmark differs by model, with the academic knowledge benchmark prominent for Llama 3.1 and HellaSwag frequent for three others.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 then identifies which protected benchmark attains the minimum lower confidence bound at the frozen operating points.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Validation–Test agreement of frozen behavioral gains. Points correspond to unique nonzero frozen interventions. The strong near-diagonal relationship is consistent across all four models.
figures.headline: Validation and held-out behavioral gains for frozen interventions lie close to the diagonal across all four models.
citing_sentences: Finally, Figure 10 exposes the validation–test relationship underlying the aggregate correlations in Section 5.2.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Specificity controls at frozen operating points. CAA is compared with norm-matched random directions (left), label-shuffled CAA directions (center), and off-target-KL-matched random directions (right). Bars report mean held-out directional behavioral gain with 95% confidence intervals for each model and across all $109$ unique nonzero frozen interventions.
figures.headline: CAA exceeds norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched null directions in every model.
citing_sentences: Table 7 reports the exact model-wise control results, while Figure 11 visualizes the same comparisons with 95% confidence intervals.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Per-model signed geometry–transfer relationship. Each panel contains all seven depth anchors and 42 ordered source–target relations per anchor. Positive association appears in every model, but with substantial dispersion.
figures.headline: Signed geometry–transfer association is positive in every model, though its dispersion is substantial.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 gives the model-wise relationships, including the corresponding $\rho_{S}$ and exact permutation $p$-values.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Causal-transfer magnitude by fractional depth. Mean absolute cross-behavior transfer peaks near fractional depth $0.42$, where the pooled mean absolute transfer is approximately $0.036$; the remaining anchors lie between approximately $0.006$ and $0.016$.
figures.headline: Mean absolute causal transfer peaks near fractional depth 0.42, at approximately 0.036, and stays between approximately 0.006 and 0.016 elsewhere.
citing_sentences: Figure 13 shows that causal-transfer magnitude itself is sharply depth dependent.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Open-ended judge trajectories by model. Scores are pooled over sycophancy, refusal, and hallucination within each model and shown for the frozen negative, baseline, and positive conditions.
figures.headline: Pooled open-ended judge scores show a single pattern across models, with differences in absolute score level and symmetry.
citing_sentences: Figure 14 provides the complementary model-wise breakdown, showing that the pooled response does not arise from a single architecture while also revealing substantial differences in absolute score level and intervention symmetry.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Open-ended sycophancy trajectories by prompt domain. NLP prompts show a stronger monotonic response than political prompts under the same frozen intervention protocol.
figures.headline: NLP sycophancy prompts show a substantially larger ordered shift under steering than political prompts, which keep the same ordering with wider uncertainty.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 separates NLP and political sycophancy prompts: the NLP subset exhibits a substantially larger ordered shift, while the political subset retains the same aggregate ordering with wider uncertainty.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: High-contrast qualitative example of sycophancy steering. Negative steering produces a more independent response, while positive steering increasingly adopts the user’s stated position. The example was selected post hoc from the frozen judged set for illustrative contrast and is not intended to represent average-case behavior.
figures.headline: Sycophancy steering in one post hoc example moves the response from independent toward adopting the user's stated position.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: High-contrast qualitative example of refusal steering. Negative steering weakens refusal and produces substantive tax-avoidance suggestions, whereas the baseline and positive conditions maintain clean refusals. The example was selected post hoc from the frozen judged set for illustrative contrast and is not intended to represent average-case behavior.
figures.headline: In one post hoc refusal example, negative steering weakens refusal and produces tax-avoidance suggestions, while baseline and positive conditions refuse cleanly.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: High-contrast qualitative example of hallucination steering. The negatively steered response challenges the premise, whereas the positively steered response makes a stronger unsupported factual claim. The example was selected post hoc from the frozen judged set for illustrative contrast and is not intended to represent average-case behavior.
figures.headline: In one post hoc hallucination example, negative steering challenges the premise while positive steering makes an unsupported factual claim.

abstract: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior–capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($\rho=0.945$), while joint behavior–capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.

sections.body: The paper treats activation steering as a constrained selection problem. It applies Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), which averages activation differences between matched positive and negative examples and adds a normalized direction to the residual stream. Validation-selected behavioral gains transfer to held-out data with Spearman rho of 0.945. Joint survival among nonzero operating points is 37.5% at a 1% budget, 72.7% at 3%, and 76.8% at 5%. CAA outperforms norm-matched, label-shuffled, and off-target-KL-matched controls, yet frozen interventions can still degrade capabilities outside the protected suite and need not transfer cleanly to open-ended generation.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Steering should be treated as a constrained selection problem with explicit capability-loss budgets, not judged on behavior alone.

sections.body: This section places the work among activation-steering methods. Representation Engineering, Activation Addition, and CAA are cited as ways to obtain activation-space directions from contrasting prompts or population-level representations. Other work scales intervention strength, composes properties, or restricts steering to putative causal subspaces, including Selective Steering, sparse mediation, and GAPS. Reliability, specificity, and capability-preservation studies are cited as motivation for explicit constraints. The authors keep CAA fixed. Their contribution is to study how its usable operating range should be selected and validated with independent held-out confirmation.
sections.heading: Background and Related Work
sections.headline: Prior steering methods change strength or space, while this paper keeps CAA fixed and studies how to select its operating range.

sections.body: For each behavior, layer-wise CAA directions are built from the vector-construction split only. The intervention layer is chosen by a coarse scan over all decoder layers at alpha of plus or minus 1, followed by a nine-layer dense search on the validation split. At that fixed layer, the coefficient is chosen from a grid running from -2 to 2 in steps of 0.5. The protected capability margin is the minimum, across MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag, of each benchmark's paired 95% lower confidence bound on accuracy change. A coefficient is feasible when this margin is at least negative epsilon, with epsilon set to 0.01, 0.03, or 0.05. The operating point is then frozen. Layer and coefficient are not jointly optimized.
sections.heading: Behavior–Capability Frontiers
sections.headline: The frontier picks, at a layer fixed on validation data, the coefficient with the largest behavior gain that meets a capability bound.

sections.body: Four models are evaluated: Llama 2 7B Chat, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, and Qwen2.5 7B Instruct. Seven behaviors come from the CAA setting, each with fixed vector, validation, and test splits; sycophancy, for example, uses 900, 300, and 300 examples. The protected benchmarks are MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag, each split into a selection set and an independent holdout. Specificity controls cover the 109 unique nonzero frozen operating points, with 20 directions per control family. Geometry is measured across 1176 ordered transfer measurements. Secondary checks use a 64-question GSM8K subset and 128 WikiText-2 windows. Open-ended generation uses 24 prompts per behavior and a language-model judge.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and three protected benchmarks share one protocol with fixed splits.

sections.body: This results section reports behavioral steerability, held-out confirmation, and audits. Selected layers fall at fractional depths of roughly 0.35 to 0.52 for three models and roughly 0.63 to 0.70 for Qwen2.5. Across 109 unique nonzero interventions, validation and held-out directional gains have Pearson r of 0.969 and Spearman rho of 0.945. Joint survival is 37.5% at the 1% budget, 72.7% at 3%, and 76.8% at 5%. Against three null families, CAA has mean held-out gain of 0.124. Signed geometry is positively associated with signed transfer, at Spearman rho of 0.290. WikiText-2 perplexity rises 6.63% on average, and refusal and hallucination do not show the ordered open-ended pattern seen for sycophancy.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Capability-constrained steering survives held-out testing for 72.7% of nonzero points at a 3% budget but only 37.5% at 1%.

sections.body: The discussion argues that behavioral steerability and a usable intervention are separate matters. CAA often gives a stable target shift at the selected layer, but capability preservation is more fragile. This explains why frontier survival changes sharply with the budget even though validation and held-out gains agree closely. Useful layers are model dependent. The controls indicate that learned directions matter beyond perturbation size or output disruption, while the geometry result shows only partial prediction of causal interaction. The frontier is therefore an evaluation-relative claim. Passing the protected suite does not guarantee preservation of WikiText-2 or GSM8K, and multiple-choice control does not guarantee the same response in free-form generation.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Under tight budgets, capability preservation rather than behavioral effect limits steering, and frontier claims hold only for the evaluated suite.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the study. Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, CAA effects transfer reliably to held-out behavioral data. The set of interventions that remains usable depends strongly on the permitted capability loss. Matched controls confirm that the effect is specific to the learned directions. Geometry, secondary-capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended audits expose limits to what a successful frontier point establishes. The answer to how far one can steer is an operating range defined by behavior, direction, layer, model, and evaluation budget, not a single steering coefficient.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The usable steering range depends on the allowed capability loss, model, behavior, layer, and direction, not on one coefficient.

sections.body: The study covers four instruction-tuned models in the 7–8B range and uses CAA throughout, so the frontier structure may not hold for larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, or other intervention families. The capability claim is limited to the benchmarks used. Preserving MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag does not imply preservation of language modeling or mathematical reasoning. The core behavioral evaluation uses binary choices, and the out-of-distribution and open-ended audits cover fewer behaviors and prompts. The judge's scores were not validated against human annotations. Cosine similarity is a coarse geometry description. The strict 1% budget is sensitive to finite-sample uncertainty, so low survival there may partly reflect conservative confidence bounds.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results cover four 7–8B models and binary-choice core tests, with an unvalidated model judge and a strict 1% budget sensitive to sampling.

sections.body: Activation steering is dual use: the same techniques can reduce or amplify behaviors such as sycophancy, hallucination, or refusal. The experiments evaluate both steering directions for this reason, and the authors state that controllability should not be conflated with alignment. The capability constraints are not deployment-safety guarantees, since a frozen operating point can satisfy the protected suite while degrading capabilities outside it. Deployment would need broader capability monitoring, task-specific safety constraints, and evaluation under the intended distribution. Behavior scores are treated as measurements under explicit rubrics, not universal definitions, and the framework is meant to make tradeoffs measurable and auditable rather than prescribe behaviors.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Steering is dual use, and passing capability constraints does not establish deployment safety.

sections.body: Generative AI assistants supported experimental scripting, debugging, visualization, and polishing of the manuscript. GPT-5.6 Sol (`gpt-5.6-sol`) was separately used as a blinded judge for the open-ended behavioral evaluations. The author directed the research, validated the experimental results, and takes full responsibility for the methodology, findings, and conclusions.
sections.heading: Use of Generative AI
sections.headline: Generative AI assistants supported scripting, debugging, visualization, and manuscript polishing, and one model served as a blinded judge.

sections.body: The appendix documents the experimental details behind the main text. Appendix A gives behavioral semantics, vector extraction, and scoring rules. Appendix B reports the full-layer localization and the behavior-selected layers, with Qwen2.5 in later layers. Appendix C lists 168 frozen claims that correspond to 109 unique nonzero interventions, with response surfaces and limiting benchmarks. Appendix D gives specificity-control details. Appendices E to G report geometry and causal transfer, secondary and out-of-distribution results, and open-ended generation. Appendix H lists software versions and compute, and states that the codebase will be released publicly.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers behavioral data and prompting, layer diagnostics, frontier and holdout results, specificity controls, geometry, open-ended details, compute, and reproducibility.
